questions.text: "What plasticity rule builds hippocampal place fields?"
"How is a memory maintained across days?"
"What can each recording modality actually resolve?"

claims.text: Dendrites initiate regenerative spikes locally, without a preceding somatic action potential.
claims.note: The split tracks stimulus modality, not preparation. Every positive report used strong, spatially concentrated, fast-onset drive; the one negative report used gradual distributed optogenetic drive. Stuart & Spruston quantify the requirement at a handful to dozens of inputs within a few ms in a localised region — which is precisely what optogenetics does not deliver. The unresolved question is which regime real synaptic bombardment resembles.

evidence.condition: strong local current injection into the dendrite
synchronous clustered glutamate uncaging on radial oblique branches
clustered input to basal dendrites; NMDA-dependent
review; quantifies the requirement as a handful to dozens of inputs in a localised region within a few ms, and asks openly whether that ever happens in vivo
optogenetic drive (~130 pA, distributed), acute slice at 34 C. Never observed dendrite-initiated dSpikes; attributes this to stimulus modality and reproduces it in a conductance-based model
treats local NMDA spikes as the established substrate of branch computation

claims.text: Whether a bAP becomes a dendritic spike is set by prior dendritic depolarisation, not by somatic spike rate.
claims.note: REGION CONFOUND, FLAGGED. Every "rate is the variable" result is L5/cortex; the only "depolarisation is the variable" result is CA1. Per the no-region-split decision these sit on one node, but the confound is total and should be resolved before either framing is treated as general. The cleanest test would be the Park ramp protocol run in L5.

evidence.condition: critical bAP frequency (~100 Hz) for distal Ca electrogenesis
ex vivo dual patch, V1 L5 — 200 Hz bAP trains engage dendritic electrogenesis, 50 Hz do not. Frequency dependence is explicit.
BAC firing — a single bAP paired with distal input suffices, which is nearer Park's rule than the frequency framing is
an isolated bAP becomes a dSpike if the distal dendrite was depolarised >=15 ms beforehand; sigmoidal dependence on stimulus distance, ~80% beyond 300 um

claims.text: A-type Kv inactivation opens the dendritic spike window and slow Nav inactivation closes it, making the dendrite a spike-rate accelerometer.
claims.note: The two channel contributions are each well established separately; the claim that their timescales jointly define a transient window is new and rests on one paper plus its model. Prime candidate for replication, and the strongest single thing to look for in vivo.

evidence.condition: 4-AP and Ba2+ raise dSpike probability, 20 nM TTX lowers it; NEURON model reproduces the failure-success-failure motif across a wide parameter range
measured the ~6-fold distal enrichment and inactivation kinetics of A-type Kv
reviews Kv channels as restricting dendritic Ca spike generation and spread, and bAP-driven reduction of subsequent Na spike probability — the ingredients, not the synthesis
Box 1 treats Kv and HCN as plateau regulators without this framing

claims.text: Plateau potentials require collision of a dendritic Na spike with glutamatergic input; coincidence of distal input with somatic spiking alone is not sufficient.
claims.note: Sharpest testable prediction in the set, and a real constraint on BTSP: during sustained fast firing the dendrite is refractory, so a distal input arriving late in a spike train cannot induce plasticity. If it holds, BTSP has a duty cycle. Untested in vivo.

evidence.condition: EFS at 0.5 s into an optogenetic ramp evoked plateaus, at 2.5 s (24 Hz sustained) did not. D-AP5, Ni2+ and TTX each reduce the plateau, so NMDAR, VGCC and Nav are all necessary
high-frequency EFS trains; stronger NMDAR dependence than Park saw with a single pulse. Induction protocol, not biology, may explain the gap
treats plateaus as reliably inducible by EC3/CA3 conjunction; no refractory window
"only a single plateau potential is sufficient" — stated without a rate caveat

claims.text: The dendritic spike is a cell-wide broadcast carrying timing but not spatial information; synapse identity is carried by glutamate-bound NMDARs.
claims.note: Answers "where is the eligibility trace" by elimination: dSpike footprints did not depend on which branch was stimulated, so voltage cannot carry it. Stuart & Spruston reach a compatible worry from the opposite direction — if dSpikes occur spontaneously from background activity, they cannot be input-specific either. Two independent routes to the same conclusion is the strongest thing this node has.

evidence.condition: bAP and dSpike spatial profiles insensitive to stimulus location; no preference for the stimulated branch
notes that spontaneous dSpikes from background synaptic activity, without clustered input, "questions their role in information processing"

reviews branch-specific plasticity and clustered spine formation as evidence that the branch is the unit of memory allocation. May be scope rather than conflict: clustered-input regime vs bAP-driven regime

claims.text: Dendritic branches act as independent computational subunits.
claims.note: Independence is conditional on impedance, not a property of branches. Wybo 2019 formalises this; Otor 2022 shows a subcompartment's morphology predicts its functional independence. So the honest form of this claim is "under conditions X" — and nobody has measured how often X holds in vivo.

evidence.condition: model; branches as independent sigmoidal subunits
branch-local spike initiation with sharp threshold in oblique dendrites
distinct motor skills engage non-overlapping apical tuft branches in vivo
apical segments carry spatial tuning different from their own soma
independence requires sufficiently high inter-branch impedance; dynamically regulated
Na spikes fail propagating from high- to low-impedance dendrites; NMDA spikes cannot leave the glutamate-release region. Compartmentalisation is a propagation failure, not a designed boundary
under bAP-driven conditions dSpikes engaged the whole apical tree, with no branch preference

claims.text: Somatic and dendritic activity are highly correlated in vivo.
claims.note: Fischer 2022 states this split explicitly with both citation lists, which is why this node exists in this form. CRITICAL SCOPE, see C7.1 — every "highly correlated" result is calcium, and Beaulieu-Laroche's own calibration shows GCaMP6f is blind to subthreshold. So the correlation claim is about suprathreshold events only, and the two camps may not be measuring the same thing.

evidence.condition: V1 L5 awake; dendritic activity in 156/157 pairs, correlation 0.542, coupling index ~0.97, unchanged by visual stimuli or locomotion
V1 L5; high but asymmetric coupling, independent of stimulation and locomotion
functional clustering during decision-making
tuft subcompartments compute independently, but independence predicted by morphology
branch-specific Ca transient prevalence predicts place field properties
dendritic spatial tuning differs from somatic during 2D navigation
names the disagreement explicitly and lists both camps without adjudicating
the same authors note compartmentalisation persists at subthreshold level, and that flexible coupling may occur on timescales or along categories GCaMP cannot resolve

claims.text: NMDA spikes are spatially restricted to the branch that generates them.
claims.note: Settled by mechanism rather than by accumulated observation: NMDAR gating needs both glutamate and depolarisation, so the event cannot exist outside the glutamate field. Kept in the tree as the calibration point for what 'settled' means here.

evidence.condition: NMDA spikes confined to the activated basal branch
NMDA spikes cannot propagate beyond the region of glutamate release, since NMDAR activation requires both glutamate and depolarisation

claims.text: Dendritic Na spikes are spatially restricted to the branch that generates them.
claims.note: SPLITTING THIS OUT CHANGED THE ANSWER. In the merged node Park's result was diluted by the NMDA and plateau evidence. Isolated, it is a head-on contradiction: Park's dSpikes are Na-mediated (abolished by 20 nM TTX) yet engaged the whole apical tree with no branch preference. Either impedance confinement fails for bAP-driven Na spikes, or locally-initiated and bAP-driven Na spikes are different objects sharing a name.

evidence.condition: Na spikes are variable triggers of axonal APs; often fail to reach the soma
Na spikes fail propagating from small high-impedance dendrites into larger low-impedance ones
fast Na dendritic spikes in basal dendrites with submillisecond precision
TTX-sensitive dSpikes engaged the entire apical tree regardless of stimulus location; no branch preference in 17 neurons

claims.text: Dendritic Ca plateau potentials are spatially restricted to the compartment that generates them.
claims.note: Probably false as written, and the interesting part is the unit. Ca spikes are restricted to a DOMAIN (the distal apical initiation zone) but propagate freely within and beyond it. If the tree keeps confusing domain-level with branch-level confinement, the fix is a `unit: branch|domain|cell` field rather than more nodes.

evidence.condition: Ca action potentials restricted to distal apical dendrites — a domain claim, not a branch claim
Box 1 — plateaus propagate through the entirety of CA1 pyramidal neurons; explicitly contrasted with local Na and NMDA events
Ca spikes deliver more charge to soma and axon than Na spikes and drive high-frequency burst firing
plateaus were global, accompanied by somatic complex spikes

claims.text: Dendritic nonlinearity primarily serves synaptic plasticity, not input integration.
claims.note: BHL's original view axis, promoted to a claim. This is the single most useful contested node in the tree — it is the disagreement that organises the two reviews, and Park's paper argues one side explicitly while flagging it as untested in vivo.

evidence.condition: under conditions where integration was linear and passive, bAPs still drove strong dendritic excitations. Authors state the plasticity-primacy reading and flag it as requiring in vivo test
distal LTP requires local dSpikes, not the bAP
bAP as the associative signal for Hebbian plasticity
argues throughout that the dendrite is a computational unit; XOR, orientation selectivity, multi-unit processor
dendritic spikes sharpen orientation tuning relative to soma — integration, not plasticity
reviews both roles as established and does not rank them

claims.text: Synaptic integration in vivo is supralinear.
claims.note: Stuart & Spruston's conclusion is that this is the wrong question: in vivo neurons perform both sub- and supra-linear integration, varying by cell type, layer and stimulus. If that is right this node should eventually be retired and replaced by "under what conditions", which is C1.1.

evidence.condition: V1 in vivo
whisker task, awake
NMDA spikes enhance AP generation during sensory input
linear integration of spine Ca signals in vivo
sublinear binocular integration
concludes both modes occur; treats the dichotomy as ill-posed

claims.text: A single neuron implements a multi-layer network.
claims.note: Mostly a modelling claim with in vivo support that is suggestive rather than direct. Note that C1.5, if true, is a serious problem for it: a two-layer network needs the hidden layer to be addressable, and a broadcast dSpike is not.

evidence.condition: two-layer model fits CA1 input-output
review; extends to ANN performance gains
morphologically detailed model learns feature binding that a point neuron cannot
reports a continuum of task specialisation across cell types rather than a categorical dendritic advantage
a spatially non-specific dSpike is a poor substrate for an addressable hidden layer

claims.text: Dendritic events causally shape behaviour.
claims.note: Stuart & Spruston's 2015 verdict was that only correlations existed. Takahashi 2016 and Maristany 2025 are the causal exceptions, and both are optogenetic manipulation of tuft activity. Still very thin for how load-bearing this claim is across the field.

evidence.condition: enhancing or suppressing apical activity shifts perceptual threshold
inhibiting apical tufts impairs relearning under new rules but not established behaviour
effect is pathway-specific (ET not IT) and context-dependent — not a general dendritic property
as of 2015, "even the best work has only shown correlations"

claims.text: BTSP is the main mechanism producing CA1 place fields.
claims.note: Magee Box 2 already is this node, with four numbered evidence lines each carrying its own caveat.

evidence.condition: single plateau produces a predictive place field in one trial
EC3 inhibition removes the reward-site overrepresentation
most new PCs show BTSP signatures during novel experience
review; Box 2 aggregates four lines with caveats
treats BTSP as the mechanism when framing credit assignment

claims.text: BTSP is the only plasticity mechanism producing CA1 place fields.
claims.note: Split from C4.1 deliberately. "Main" and "only" have different evidence and must not share a node — Magee concedes under 25% of PCs lack BTSP hallmarks and explicitly leaves this open, while Sheffield & Dombeck offer a clustered-synapse alternative.

evidence.condition: "Questions remain as to whether BTSP is the sole synaptic plasticity mechanism"; <25% of PCs lack the signatures
already-strengthened or clustered synapses can drive place cell activity via local dSpikes
BTSP but not STDP accounts for place field shifting dynamics

claims.text: The BTSP rule is asymmetric in CA1 and symmetric in CA3.
claims.note: If true, the plasticity rule is tuned to network function rather than fixed by biochemistry — which is a much stronger claim than it looks, and rests on one paper.

evidence.condition: symmetric ~5 s window at CA3-CA3 recurrent synapses
asymmetric, projecting further backward
review; links the asymmetry to prediction vs attractor stability

claims.text: EC3 input is a target signal, not an error signal.
claims.note: Magee's argument is negative evidence with a clear logic — EC3 activity stayed constant while CA1 adapted, which is not what an error signal does. The predictive-coding models require error. Chavlis & Poirazi state outright the question is unresolved.

evidence.condition: EC3 peak at salient regions persisted for the whole session instead of decaying as CA1 adapted
dendritic voltage as prediction, somatic spike as ground truth; requires an error
section 2.5.2 frames association vs prediction error as unresolved: "remains to be seen"
distal apical responses to pattern-violating stimuli increase as somatic responses adapt — error-like

claims.text: Dendrites implement backpropagation-like, neuron-specific credit assignment.
claims.note: Fischer 2022 says plainly this "remains untested", and describes the BCI design built to test it. Worth watching as the node most likely to move in the next two years.

evidence.condition: segregated dendrites approximate backprop error
burst-dependent plasticity coordinates learning in hierarchical circuits
apical dendrites process instructive signals in vectorised format during a BCI task
states the hypothesis "remains untested" and lays out the BCI design intended to test it
argues EC3 cannot be neuron-specific — stochastic, and each axon innervates thousands of CA1 cells; proposes stable residual weights supply the specificity instead

claims.text: Memory persists through stabilised synaptic weights.
claims.note: The classical position. Magee Box 5 is written explicitly as a contrast against it.

evidence.condition: foundational assumption of the archicortex model
attractor memory via fixed weights
Box 5 — "Contrasts with concepts based on complete reactivation ... via stable synaptic weights"
even stable PCs required new BTSP each day; weights decayed or were overwritten overnight

claims.text: Memory persists via a raised likelihood of new neuron-specific plasticity.
claims.note: The positive form of C6.1's negation, and a genuinely new proposal. Rests on the residual subthreshold depolarisation that lowers plateau threshold at particular locations. One lab.

evidence.condition: stable PC population expanded ~3-fold over a week; residual amplitude grew with days
experience-dependent place cell referencing
review; proposes it as the solution to the stability-plasticity dilemma

claims.text: Dendritic calcium signals report dendritic voltage.
claims.note: THIS NODE RE-WEIGHTS MOST OTHERS. Beaulieu-Laroche calibrated it directly and found subthreshold depolarisation produces negligible GCaMP6f signal — so calcium reports suprathreshold electrogenesis, not membrane potential. Park adds a spatial argument: Ca diffuses ~2 um in 100 ms while electrical length constants exceed 100 um, so the two signals have different spatial structure by construction. Most in vivo dendritic literature is calcium. Every claim above resting on calcium in vivo inherits this scope.

evidence.condition: ex vivo dual patch + GCaMP6f — subthreshold produces negligible dF/F, suprathreshold electrogenesis produces significant dF/F. Calcium reports electrogenesis specifically
Ca buffered diffusion <20 um2/s gives ~2 um spread per 100 ms vs >100 um electrical length constants; calls for simultaneous voltage and calcium imaging to settle it
names calcium temporal resolution and fluorescence nonlinearity as formidable obstacles
treats in vivo calcium imaging as evidence for dendritic spikes throughout

claims.text: Slice dendritic excitability at room temperature reflects physiological behaviour.
claims.note: Park measured this directly and the effect is large. Several classic dendritic results were collected at room temperature, so this is not a pedantic node.

evidence.condition: dSpike probability 16% at 34 C vs 50% at 24 C (any bAP); authors propose this explains discrepancies with earlier room-temperature bAP propagation measurements

claims.text: Anaesthesia preserves dendritic integration.
claims.note: Stuart & Spruston raise this as an unresolved confound and note that in vitro work shows most anaesthetics degrade active dendritic membrane properties. A large share of the in vivo dendritic literature is anaesthetized.

evidence.condition: flags anaesthetics as a possible source of apparent disagreement; cites in vitro evidence that most anaesthetics negatively affect active dendritic membrane properties
direct measurement of anaesthetic effects on dendritic properties
general anaesthesia decouples apical input from somatic output

claims.text: Optogenetic dendritic stimulation approximates physiological synaptic drive.
claims.note: The methodological node underneath C1.1. Park estimates ~130 pA of dendritic CheRiff current, far below the injected currents that trigger local Na spikes in patch studies — which is either the reason their result differs, or the reason their result is the more physiological one. Nobody has measured which.

evidence.condition: estimates dendritic CheRiff currents at ~130 pA and shows in simulation that the absence of dendrite-initiated dSpikes follows from the gradual, weak, distributed stimulus
"activation is nonetheless artificial"; in vitro studies describe possible computations, not the ones the brain uses

papers.title: Dendrocentric learning for synthetic intelligence
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence now advances by performing twice as many floating-point multiplications every two months, but the semiconductor industry tiles twice as many multipliers on a chip every two years. Moreover, the returns from tiling these multipliers ever more densely now diminish because signals must travel relatively farther and farther. Although travel can be shortened by stacking tiled multipliers in a three-dimensional chip, such a solution acutely reduces the available surface area for dissipating heat. Here I propose to transcend this three-dimensional thermal constraint by moving away from learning with synapses to learning with dendrites. Synaptic inputs are not weighted precisely but rather ordered meticulously along a short stretch of dendrite, termed dendrocentric learning. With the help of a computational model of a dendrite and a conceptual model of a ferroelectric device that emulates it, I illustrate how dendrocentric learning artificial intelligence—or synthetic intelligence for short—could run not with megawatts in the cloud but rather with watts on a smartphone.
papers.tldr: The concept of dendrocentric learning artificial intelligence is proposed to replace synaptocentric learning, reducing the energy use requirement and removing the thermal constraint.

papers.title: Dendritic, delayed, stochastic CaMKII activation in behavioural time scale plasticity
papers.abstract: Abstract Behavioural time scale plasticity (BTSP) is non-Hebbian plasticity induced by integrating presynaptic and postsynaptic components separated by a behaviourally relevant time scale (seconds) 1 . BTSP in hippocampal CA1 neurons underlies place cell formation. However, the molecular mechanisms that enable synapse-specific plasticity on a behavioural time scale are unknown. Here we show that BTSP can be induced in a single dendritic spine using two-photon glutamate uncaging paired with postsynaptic current injection temporally separated by a behavioural time scale. Using an improved Ca 2+ /calmodulin-dependent kinase II (CaMKII) sensor, we did not detect CaMKII activation during this BTSP induction. Instead, we observed dendritic, delayed and stochastic CaMKII activation (DDSC) associated with Ca 2+ influx and plateau potentials 10–100 s after BTSP induction. DDSC required both presynaptic and postsynaptic activity, which suggests that CaMKII can integrate these two signals. Also, optogenetically blocking CaMKII 15–30 s after the BTSP protocol inhibited synaptic potentiation, which indicated that DDSC is an essential mechanism of BTSP. IP 3 -dependent intracellular Ca 2+ release facilitated both DDSC and BTSP. Thus, our study suggests that non-synapse-specific CaMKII activation provides an instructive signal with an extensive time window over tens of seconds during BTSP.
papers.tldr: This study suggests that non-synapse-specific CaMKII activation provides an instructive signal with an extensive time window over tens of seconds during BTSP, findings that clarify the mechanisms that underlie place cell formation.

papers.title: Dependence of EPSP Efficacy on Synapse Location in Neocortical Pyramidal Neurons
papers.abstract: Neurons receive thousands of synaptic inputs throughout elaborate dendritic trees. Here we determine the somatic impact of excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) generated at known dendritic sites in neocortical pyramidal neurons. As inputs became more distal, somatic EPSP amplitude decreased, whereas use-dependent depression increased. Despite marked attenuation (>40-fold), when coactivated within a narrow time window (approximately 10 milliseconds), distal EPSPs could directly influence action potential output following dendritic spike generation. These findings reveal that distal EPSPs are ineffective sources of background somatic excitation, but through coincidence detection have a powerful transient signaling role.
papers.tldr: The findings reveal that distal EPSPs are ineffective sources of background somatic excitation, but through coincidence detection have a powerful transient signaling role.

papers.title: Distal tuft dendrites predict properties of new hippocampal place fields
papers.abstract: Hippocampal pyramidal neurons support episodic memory by integrating complementary information streams into new “place fields.” Distal tuft dendrites have been proposed to drive place field formation via dendritic plateau potentials. However, the relationship between distal dendritic and somatic activity is unknown in vivo. Here, we gained simultaneous optical access to distal tuft dendrites and their soma in head-fixed mice navigating virtual reality environments. While distal tuft dendrites rarely express local peri-formation plateau potentials, the timing and extent of their recruitment predict properties of resultant somatic place fields. Following somatic place field formation, distal tuft dendrites readily express plateau potentials as well as local place fields that are back shifted relative to that of their soma. Distal tuft dendrites may therefore undergo local plasticity during somatic place field formation. Through direct in vivo observation, we provide an updated dendritic basis for hippocampal feature selectivity during navigational learning.
papers.tldr: Through direct in vivo observation, this work provides an updated dendritic basis for hippocampal feature selectivity during navigational learning by gaining simultaneous optical access to distal tuft dendrites and their soma in head-fixed mice navigating virtual reality environments.

papers.title: Distribution of bursting neurons in the CA1 region and the subiculum of the rat hippocampus
papers.abstract: We performed patch-clamp recordings from morphologically identified and anatomically mapped pyramidal neurons of the ventral hippocampus to test the hypothesis that bursting neurons are distributed on a gradient from the CA2/CA1 border (proximal) through the subiculum (distal), with more bursting observed at distal locations. We find that the well-defined morphological boundaries between the hippocampal subregions CA1 and subiculum do not correspond to abrupt changes in electrophysiological properties. Rather, we observed that the percentage of bursting neurons is linearly correlated with position in the proximal-distal axis across the CA1 and the subiculum, the percentages of bursting neurons being 10% near the CA1-CA2 border, 24% at the CA1-subiculum border, and higher than 50% in the distal subiculum. The distribution of bursting neurons was paralleled by a gradient in afterdepolarization (ADP) amplitude. We also tested the hypothesis that there was an association between bursting and two previously described morphologically distinct groups of pyramidal neurons (twin and single apical dendrites) in the CA1 region. We found no difference in output mode between single and twin apical dendrite morphologies, which was consistent with the observation that the two morphologies were equally distributed across the transverse axis of the CA1 region. Taken together with the known organization of connections from CA3 to CA1 and CA1 to subiculum, our results indicate that bursting neurons are most likely to be connected to regular spiking neurons and vice versa.
papers.tldr: The results indicate that bursting neurons are most likely to be connected to regular spiking neurons and vice versa.

papers.title: Distinct synaptic plasticity rules operate across dendritic compartments in vivo during learning
papers.abstract: Synaptic plasticity underlies learning by modifying specific synaptic inputs to reshape neural activity and behavior. However, the rules governing which synapses will undergo different forms of plasticity in vivo during learning and whether these rules are uniform within individual neurons remain unclear. Using in vivo longitudinal imaging with single-synapse resolution in the mouse motor cortex during motor learning, we found that apical and basal dendrites of layer 2/3 (L2/3) pyramidal neurons showed distinct activity-dependent synaptic plasticity rules. The strengthening of apical and of basal synapses is predicted by local coactivity with nearby synapses and activity coincident with postsynaptic action potentials, respectively. Blocking postsynaptic spiking diminished basal synaptic potentiation without affecting apical plasticity. Thus, individual neurons use multiple activity-dependent plasticity rules in a compartment-specific manner in vivo during learning.
papers.tldr: Using in vivo longitudinal imaging with single synapse resolution in the mouse motor cortex during motor learning, it is found that apical and basal dendrites of L2/3 pyramidal neurons showed distinct activity-dependent synaptic plasticity rules.

papers.title: Distribution and Function of HCN Channels in the Apical Dendritic Tuft of Neocortical Pyramidal Neurons
papers.abstract: The apical tuft is the most remote area of the dendritic tree of neocortical pyramidal neurons. Despite its distal location, the apical dendritic tuft of layer 5 pyramidal neurons receives substantial excitatory synaptic drive and actively processes corticocortical input during behavior. The properties of the voltage-activated ion channels that regulate synaptic integration in tuft dendrites have, however, not been thoroughly investigated. Here, we use electrophysiological and optical approaches to examine the subcellular distribution and function of hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated nonselective cation (HCN) channels in rat layer 5B pyramidal neurons. Outside-out patch recordings demonstrated that the amplitude and properties of ensemble HCN channel activity were uniform in patches excised from distal apical dendritic trunk and tuft sites. Simultaneous apical dendritic tuft and trunk whole-cell current-clamp recordings revealed that the pharmacological blockade of HCN channels decreased voltage compartmentalization and enhanced the generation and spread of apical dendritic tuft and trunk regenerative activity. Furthermore, multisite two-photon glutamate uncaging demonstrated that HCN channels control the amplitude and duration of synaptically evoked regenerative activity in the distal apical dendritic tuft. In contrast, at proximal apical dendritic trunk and somatic recording sites, the blockade of HCN channels decreased excitability. Dynamic-clamp experiments revealed that these compartment-specific actions of HCN channels were heavily influenced by the local and distributed impact of the high density of HCN channels in the distal apical dendritic arbor. The properties and subcellular distribution pattern of HCN channels are therefore tuned to regulate the interaction between integration compartments in layer 5B pyramidal neurons.
papers.tldr: Electrophysiological and optical approaches are used to examine the subcellular distribution and function of hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated nonselective cation channels in rat layer 5B pyramidal neurons and demonstrate that HCN channels control the amplitude and duration of synaptically evoked regenerative activity in the distal apical dendritic tuft.

papers.title: Dendritic spikes induce single-burst long-term potentiation
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: The hippocampus is essential for episodic memory, which requires single-trial learning. Although long-term potentiation (LTP) of synaptic strength is a candidate mechanism for learning, it is typically induced by using repeated synaptic activation to produce precisely timed, high-frequency, or rhythmic firing. Here we show that hippocampal synapses potentiate robustly in response to strong activation by a single burst. The induction mechanism of this single-burst LTP requires activation of NMDA receptors, L-type voltage-gated calcium channels, and dendritic spikes. Thus, dendritic spikes are a critical trigger for a form of LTP that is consistent with the function of the hippocampus in episodic memory.

papers.title: Dendritic Voltage-Gated Ion Channels Regulate the Action Potential Firing Mode of Hippocampal CA1 Pyramidal Neurons
papers.abstract: The role of dendritic voltage-gated ion channels in the generation of action potential bursting was investigated using whole cell patch-clamp recordings from the soma and dendrites of CA1 pyramidal neurons located in hippocampal slices of adult rats. Under control conditions somatic current injections evoked single action potentials that were associated with an afterhyperpolarization (AHP). After localized application of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) to the distal apical dendritic arborization, the same current injections resulted in the generation of an afterdepolarization (ADP) and multiple action potentials. This burst firing was not observed after localized application of 4-AP to the soma/proximal dendrites. The dendritic 4-AP application allowed large-amplitude Na(+)-dependent action potentials, which were prolonged in duration, to backpropagate into the distal apical dendrites. No change in action potential backpropagation was seen with proximal 4-AP application. Both the ADP and action potential bursting could be inhibited by the bath application of nonspecific concentrations of divalent Ca(2+) channel blockers (NiCl and CdCl). Ca(2+) channel blockade also reduced the dendritic action potential duration without significantly affecting spike amplitude. Low concentrations of TTX (10-50 nM) also reduced the ability of the CA1 neurons to fire in the busting mode. This effect was found to be the result of an inhibition of backpropagating dendritic action potentials and could be overcome through the coordinated injection of transient, large-amplitude depolarizing current into the dendrite. Dendritic current injections were able to restore the burst firing mode (represented as a large ADP) even in the presence of high concentrations of TTX (300-500 microM). These data suggest the role of dendritic Na(+) channels in bursting is to allow somatic/axonal action potentials to backpropagate into the dendrites where they then activate dendritic Ca(2+) channels. Although it appears that most Ca(2+) channel subtypes are important in burst generation, blockade of T- and R-type Ca(2+) channels by NiCl (75 microM) inhibited action potential bursting to a greater extent than L-channel (10 microM nimodipine) or N-, P/Q-type (1 microM omega-conotoxin MVIIC) Ca(2+) channel blockade. This suggest that the Ni-sensitive voltage-gated Ca(2+) channels have the most important role in action potential burst generation. In summary, these data suggest that the activation of dendritic voltage-gated Ca(2+) channels, by large-amplitude backpropagating spikes, provides a prolonged inward current that is capable of generating an ADP and burst of multiple action potentials in the soma of CA1 pyramidal neurons. Dendritic voltage-gated ion channels profoundly regulate the processing and storage of incoming information in CA1 pyramidal neurons by modulating the action potential firing mode from single spiking to burst firing.
papers.tldr: The activation of dendritic voltage-gated Ca(2+) channels, by large-amplitude backpropagating spikes, provides a prolonged inward current that is capable of generating an ADP and burst of multiple action potentials in the soma of CA1 pyramidal neurons.

papers.title: Distinct CA3 inputs differentially shape the learning-dependent evolution of right CA1 spatial maps
papers.abstract: Spatial maps in hippocampal CA1 arise from place fields that support memory and navigation, yet how upstream inputs shape these maps during learning remains unclear. Here we show that CA3 projections from the left and right hemispheres make distinct contributions to right CA1 spatial representations as animals become familiar with a new environment. Using two-photon calcium imaging and optogenetic inhibition in mice navigating virtual tracks, we monitored and perturbed CA3 inputs converging onto CA1. CA1 spatial maps were initially inaccurate but stabilized within ~10 laps, marking a transition from an early learning phase to a later stable phase. During early learning, right-origin CA3 inputs exerted stronger influence on the refinement of spatial coding, whereas left-origin inputs became more important for maintaining stable representations later. Axonal recordings revealed a corresponding shift in spatial activity between right and left CA3 inputs over time. Together, these results reveal that distinct CA3 inputs dynamically redistribute their influence during learning to coordinate the refinement and stabilization of right CA1 spatial maps. Neural mechanisms underlying spatial dynamics across distinct memory phases are not fully understood. Here authors show that distinct inputs from the left and right CA3 dynamically shape CA1 spatial maps, shifting their influence from early refinement to later stability as animals learn a new environment.

papers.title: Distinct sensorimotor encoding in tuft dendrites and somata associated with action, correction, and learning
papers.abstract: Frontal cortex plays critical roles in action control and motor skill learning. Within the layer 1 apical tuft dendrites of layer 5 (L5) neurons in frontal cortex, precise input patterns and back-propagating action potentials can trigger powerful regenerative events that may be essential for flexible computation and learning. However, it remains unclear whether tuft activity in frontal cortical L5 circuits encodes sensorimotor information that differs from the information conveyed by their outputs to downstream targets. Using longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging, we investigated sensorimotor encoding in the apical tuft dendrites and somata of L5 extratelencephalic (ET) neurons in the frontal cortex of mice during learning of a discrete change to a cued dexterous action. During learning, movement errors either triggered corrective action or did not, allowing us to dissociate error signals from signals selective for corrective action. Somatic activity tracked both instructional cues and action, whereas tuft activity predominantly tracked instructional cues. Movement errors during learning revealed additional distinct tuft activity that was selectively associated with corrective actions. Furthermore, learning induced divergent changes in the response gain and net selectivity of tuft dendrites compared to somata. Our measurements uncover systematic differences between the tuft dendrites and somata in sensorimotor selectivity, sensitivity to corrective action, and functional plasticity, providing a foundation for investigating the contributions of dendritic computation to motor skill learning.
papers.tldr: These measurements uncover systematic differences between the tuft dendrites and somata in sensorimotor selectivity, sensitivity to corrective action, and functional plasticity, providing a foundation for investigating the contributions of dendritic computation to motor skill learning.

papers.title: Distinct types of dendritic Ca2+ spikes in CA3 pyramidal neurons associated with neuronal activity changes during navigation
papers.abstract: Active dendrites enrich single-neuron computations by performing nonlinear input integration, including generation of dendritic spikes. Diverse dendritic spike types have been found in various cortical neuron classes in vitro; however, their in vivo prevalence and roles remained elusive. We measured calcium activity in apical dendrites and soma of pyramidal cells in the hippocampal area CA3 (CA3PCs) during virtual navigation in mice. Although dendritic activity was generally synchronous with the soma, their correlation decreased with dendritic distance. We identified two types of regenerative dendritic activities: slow, large-amplitude global Ca 2+ events representing putative Ca 2+ plateaus and fast Ca 2+ events with large dendrite-to-soma attenuation, representing putative dendritically initiated Ca 2+ spikes. Ca 2+ plateaus contributed to spatially tuned activity but only occasionally induced new place fields, suggesting conditional induction of synaptic plasticity. In contrast, fast Ca 2+ spikes were often followed by transient increase in somatic activity without spatial tuning, suggesting increased excitatory inputs or excitability. Our results unveil previously unidentified mechanisms whereby dendritic activity shapes output of CA3PCs in vivo.

evidence.prep: awake mice performing virtual navigation task

papers.significance: Two distinct dendritic Ca²⁺ spike types in CA3 pyramidal cells differentially shape somatic output in vivo, establishing that dendrite-type-specific regenerative events selectively gate plasticity versus excitability.
